question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two equity funds over the past five years. Here are the annual returns: Fund X: 8%, 12%, -5%, 15%, 10% Fund Y: 10%, 9%, -3%, 18%, 8%
Calculate the average annual return for Fund X.

explanation.text: The Logic: Arithmetic average annual return = (sum of annual returns) / number of years. For Fund X: (8% + 12% - 5% + 15% + 10%) / 5 = 40% / 5 = 8%. The Trap: 8.5% tempts candidates who accidentally use Fund Y's sum or mis-add; 7.5% tempts those who treat the -5% as -10%; 9% tempts those who drop a period or round prematurely. All three distractors reward careless arithmetic. Cross-Exam Context: Arithmetic vs geometric mean return distinction is a staple of NISM-XV (Research Analyst), NISM-XXI-B (PMS Managers), and NISM-VIII (Equity Derivatives) portfolio modules. Distributor's Pro-Tip: Never quote the arithmetic average to a client as the 'annualised return' on a PMS strategy - SEBI disclosure standards require CAGR (geometric), and the arithmetic number is always higher; clients who later see the CAGR on the factsheet feel mis-sold.
